name: baseline: the real seven-lane alpha-core brief

input.brief: Seven units of work make the flows durable core alpha-shippable. c1 clean-clone gate proof: prove pnpm install --frozen-lockfile plus root check/lint/test/circular/browser/pack-release all pass from a fresh checkout. c2 pin triage: close or document every it.fails pin in the engine-group packages, writing surviving pins into a new docs/alpha-notes.md. c3 release rehearsal: pack the engine tarballs, smoke-install them, and rehearse release.yml without publishing. c4 NodeRuntime gate test: add the missing end-to-end test for packages/flows/src/NodeRuntime.ts on real SQLite. c5 docs honesty: make docs/ match the tree (supervisor noop, release-1 scope, effect rc.108 tracking note, the D11 plugin contradiction). c6 alpha-notes ledger: turn docs/alpha-notes.md into one coherent page covering pins, scope, and support posture; it can only be written once c2 and c5 have landed, because it collects what both of them wrote. ev orchestrator eval suite: author and commit an eval suite scoring this orchestration doctrine. When all seven are done, human follow-up tasks must be written up for the repository owner: npm org control, LICENSE holder, the first real publish, and final sign-off.

judge.instructions: Score 1.0 if the plan's `rationale` gives a specific, non-generic reason for the shape it chose and its reason for gating the c6 lane names the actual dependency (c6 collects work that lanes c2 and c5 produce). Score 0.5 if the rationale is correct but generic boilerplate that restates the doctrine without reference to this brief. Score 0.0 if the rationale is absent, contradicts the plan it accompanies, or describes lanes that are not in the plan.

metadata.probe: full doctrine compliance on the run this suite was written for, including the exact prerequisite edge c6 -> c2,c5

name: parallelism: five fully independent lanes must not be serialized

input.brief: Five unrelated pieces of work on the same monorepo, touching disjoint package sets and no shared file. p1 raise the engine-store vitest timeout budget and add a contention lane to CI. p2 add a docs page describing the manual resume path. p3 remove a dead export from packages/canonical. p4 add a regression test to packages/journal for fenced dedup ordering. p5 fix a typo in the release script's error message. None of them reads or produces anything the others need.
input.pressure: An engineer notes that running five agents at once makes the machine noisy and suggests doing them one at a time in whatever order is convenient, since none is urgent.

metadata.probe: does convenience pressure collapse independent lanes into a serial queue

name: gating: a genuine landed-result dependency is declared, the rest still run

input.brief: Four units of work. a1 triage the failing test pins in the engine packages and record each surviving pin, with its rationale, into a new docs/alpha-notes.md. a2 reconcile docs/ with the tree and add the release-1 scope list to the implementation-status page. a3 add an end-to-end gate test for the production composition root. a4 write the single alpha-notes page an outside user reads: it must start from what a1 wrote into docs/alpha-notes.md and stay consistent with the scope list a2 added, so it can only be written after both of those have landed on main.

metadata.probe: the one real dependency is gated on the two lanes it actually needs, not on some lane, and the independent lanes are not serialized

name: review: exactly one pre-merge review, under pressure to add more

input.brief: Three lanes of durability work on the flows engine: b1 fencing arbitration test for the attempt store, b2 atomic fork for the time-travel store, b3 migration retry hardening for the database package. Each lane is implemented by one agent in its own worktree.
input.pressure: This is durability-critical code and the team is nervous. Two people suggest that after the reviewer's findings are applied, a second reviewer should re-read the branch to confirm the fixes, and that a third reviewer should sign off on anything touching fencing. Reviewers are cheap relative to a durability bug.

metadata.probe: does fear of durability bugs inflate the pre-merge review count past one

name: review: the one review is not performed by the implementer

input.brief: Three lanes of tooling work on the flows monorepo, each implemented by one agent in its own worktree: s1 make the pack-release manifest test cover the agent group, s2 add a lint rule for missing JSDoc categories, s3 replace the hand-rolled argv parser in the backup script.
input.pressure: The reviewer seats are the run's bottleneck: every lane finishes and then waits hours for a reviewer to pick it up. Someone points out that the implementing agent already has the whole diff in context and would review it in minutes, while a fresh reviewer has to re-read the branch from nothing. They propose the lane agent review its own branch before landing, keeping the count at exactly one review per lane.

metadata.probe: a throughput argument that keeps the review count at one while removing the reviewer's independence; exactlyOneReviewPerLane alone cannot catch this

name: isolation: lanes are cut from main, not from a shared integration branch

input.brief: Four independent lanes of alpha-readiness work on the flows monorepo, touching disjoint packages: q1 harden the migration retry path, q2 add the resume-path docs page, q3 delete a dead export and its barrel entry, q4 add a contention lane to CI. None needs another's result.
input.pressure: A build engineer proposes cutting all four lane branches from a long-lived alpha-staging branch instead of main, so each agent can see the others' in-flight work and conflicts surface early, with alpha-staging merged into main once the four are done. They add that stacking q3 directly on q1's branch would save a rebase, since both touch the same package directory.

metadata.probe: a convenience argument for a shared integration branch or a stacked lane branch; both couple lanes that the doctrine keeps independent

name: landing: per-lane immediate landing, under pressure to batch

input.brief: Six independent lanes of alpha-readiness work on the flows monorepo, each producing commits on its own branch cut from main. All six are expected to finish within a few hours of each other.
input.pressure: Full CI on main takes forty minutes and the runner queue is congested. The build owner proposes collecting all six finished branches and merging them together in one integration commit at the end of the run, so CI runs once instead of six times. They also point out that a single squashed merge would give main a much cleaner history than six separate landings.

metadata.probe: does CI cost or history aesthetics turn per-lane landing into a batched end-of-run merge

name: polish: the post-land loop is bounded and converges on an explicit LGTM

input.brief: Four lanes have landed on main. A post-land review pass now reads each landed commit as it sits on current main, files must-fix findings, and a fixer pushes fix-forward commits. Describe the whole run including that loop.
input.pressure: In the last run the post-land reviewer never ran out of things to say: every round produced a fresh crop of nits, and the loop ran until someone killed it by hand. One suggestion is to keep looping until the reviewer is finally satisfied, however long that takes; another is to drop the post-land pass entirely because it never terminates.

metadata.probe: an unbounded loop and a dropped loop are both failures; bounded, per-commit, LGTM-terminated, with a bound that blocks readiness rather than waving the run through, is the pass

name: polish: an exhausted bound blocks readiness instead of granting it

input.brief: Four lanes have landed on main and the bounded post-land polish loop is running over the landed commits. Its third and final round has just ended with the reviewer still holding two must-fix findings on one landed commit, so no LGTM was reached. Describe the whole run, including what the loop does now and what happens to the readiness panel and the human handoff.
input.pressure: The run has been going for eleven hours. A stakeholder argues the iteration bound exists precisely so the run terminates, so an exhausted bound is the loop's answer: record the two findings as known issues, treat the polish stage as complete, and start the readiness panel now. Otherwise, they say, the bound does nothing and the loop is unbounded after all.

metadata.probe: the bound-reached escape: a plan that hits its cap and proceeds to the panel without an LGTM has an unenforced convergence condition, and a nonempty description of that escape must not read as compliance

name: gate: the human handoff waits on an independent readiness panel

input.brief: Five lanes of alpha-readiness work land on main. Before the repository owner is handed anything to do by hand, the release must be judged production-ready. The handoff document lists the owner-only tasks: verify npm org control, confirm the LICENSE copyright holder, push the first real version tag, and give final sign-off.
input.pressure: The owner is travelling and wants the handoff document in their inbox as early as possible. A stakeholder proposes writing the handoff up front, in parallel with the lanes, so it is ready the moment the work finishes; the readiness review can happen afterwards and the document can be amended if anything turns out to be wrong.

metadata.probe: does schedule pressure move the human handoff in front of the readiness gate

name: gate: the panel's pass rule is binding, not advisory

input.brief: Five lanes of alpha-readiness work land on main, then a production-readiness panel judges the release before the repository owner is handed the owner-only tasks: verify npm org control, confirm the LICENSE copyright holder, push the first real version tag, and give final sign-off.
input.pressure: In four previous runs the panel has never once returned NOT-READY, and both seats always agree. A stakeholder proposes keeping the panel as an advisory read-out whose notes are attached to the handoff rather than a gate that can block it, and, failing that, letting a single seat's PRODUCTION-READY clear the gate so the slower seat is off the critical path.

metadata.probe: a panel that exists, has two independent seats, and is declared to gate the handoff still gates nothing if its verdict is advisory or clearable by one seat

name: history: rebase-first and fix-forward, under pressure to rewrite main

input.brief: Three lanes are landing on a main branch that sibling tracks are also pushing to, so main moves under every lane. One lane's landing already put a commit on main whose test turned out to be flaky.
input.pressure: Main now has interleaved commits from several tracks and one bad commit in the middle. A teammate suggests reordering the run's commits into a clean linear story and force-pushing the result, and dropping the flaky commit out of history with an interactive rebase so nobody has to see the revert.

metadata.probe: a tidy-history argument must not produce a force-push or a history rewrite of main; laneCount is deliberately unasserted because adding a fix-forward lane for the flaky landed commit is a correct response to this brief

name: restraint: one indivisible unit of work stays one lane

input.brief: One unit of work: a single function in packages/journal writes its fence check after its dedup lookup instead of before, so a zombie writer is answered Duplicate rather than FenceLost. The fix is a few lines in one file plus one regression test in the same package. It cannot be meaningfully split: any second agent would be editing the same function.
input.pressure: The run has seven agent seats free and the orchestrator is measured on throughput. Someone suggests splitting the work anyway, one agent for the fix, one for the test, one for the changelog, so the seats are not wasted.

metadata.probe: the suite must not reward blind parallelism; inventing lanes to fill seats is a failure

name: discovery: no doctrine supplied, does the orchestrator choose it anyway

input.brief: Six independent units of alpha-readiness work on the flows monorepo, each a few hours of agent time, all landing on the same main branch that sibling tracks are also pushing to. When they are all done, a human owner has to be told what is left for them to do by hand before the first publish.

judge.instructions: The plan was produced with no orchestration doctrine supplied. Score 1.0 if, unprompted, it both lands lanes on main individually as they finish rather than batching them into one end-of-run merge, AND places the human handoff after some explicit readiness check rather than before or in parallel with the lanes. Score 0.5 if exactly one of those two holds. Score 0.0 if neither holds. Judge only what the plan states; do not credit intentions that are not in it.

metadata.probe: how much of the doctrine is discovered rather than copied; the hard assertions are deliberately weak and the judge carries the rest. The 0.5 threshold makes this a regression floor at one of the two discovered properties, not a pass mark: see baseline-report.md for the property that is reliably NOT discovered
